strengths: Rigorous expert annotation at scale: 100 licensed professionals with verified credentials providing 2,000 evaluations with high inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's α ≥ 0.7) and rich span-level annotations (median 576.5 words per rationale)

Clinically grounded evaluation rubric: Six dimensions informed by psychology literature capture both quality and safety concerns, addressing gaps in existing medical QA benchmarks that focus on multiple-choice tasks

Important negative result on LLM-as-Judge: Systematic demonstration that LLM-based evaluators systematically overrate responses, miss safety concerns, and fail to detect problematic content at sentence level—challenging popular automated evaluation approaches

Dual-component design providing both breadth and depth: COUNSELBENCH-EVAL (2,000 expert evaluations) combined with COUNSELBENCH-ADV (120 adversarial questions) grounded in observed failures provides comprehensive coverage
Real-world grounding: Uses authentic questions from CounselChat (actual mental health platform), ensuring ecological validity and practical relevance to help-seeking scenarios
Comprehensive reproducibility: Detailed appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, compute resources, credential verification procedures, and IRB approval support reproducibility and transparency
Diverse expert panel: 32 distinct license types and 43 specialization areas ensure evaluation reflects diverse real-world clinical practice
Commitment to community: Public release of COUNSELBENCH-EVAL and COUNSELBENCH-ADV as shared resources
weaknesses: Limited scope of core evaluation: Only 100 base questions and 3 LLMs (GPT-4, LLaMA-3.3, Gemini) directly evaluated on COUNSELBENCH-EVAL, limiting generalizability across question diversity and model families; missing recent models

Selection bias in dataset construction: Exclusion of sensitive topics (LGBTQ+, human sexuality, spirituality, religion) due to review concerns creates coverage gaps in important mental health domains; using 'most upvoted' responses as gold standard may favor consensus over clinical quality

Adversarial dataset validation concerns: Only 72.9% agreement between GPT-4.1 and human validation on 96/3,240 responses; despite acknowledgment, all analyses rely on GPT-4.1 labels for the remaining responses without extended human validation

Annotator variability inadequately addressed: Statistically significant differences in scores by experience level (less-experienced annotators assign higher Empathy scores); time spent correlates with Medical Advice and Factual Consistency ratings; implications for score validity underexplored

Artificial experimental constraints: 250-word response limit via rejection sampling may not reflect natural model outputs; prompt design is minimal with no sensitivity analysis; multiple statistical tests without multiple-comparison correction increase Type I error risk

Limited analysis of model performance variation: Paper identifies performance differences but lacks deep explanation of *why* models differ or which model properties drive success/failure on different dimensions

Incomplete exploration of model improvement: Few-shot experiments show minimal improvements (Table 3) without investigation into causes or implications; limited actionable recommendations for addressing identified failure modes
Moderate human baseline: Human therapist responses are from pre-2022 CounselChat (informal context); some score lower than LLMs on several dimensions, limiting their utility as ground truth

strengths: Addresses timely and important real-world problem in high-stakes mental health domain
Rigorous expert annotation methodology with 100 licensed professionals and detailed written rationales (median 576.5 words) demonstrating strong engagement
Strong inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's α ≥ 0.7) indicating high annotation quality
Clinically grounded evaluation rubric with six well-motivated dimensions based on clinical psychology literature
Valuable and novel finding that LLM judges systematically overrate responses and miss safety concerns, with clear evidence of model-specific ranking divergence
Effective adversarial benchmark component revealing consistent, model-specific failure patterns
Excellent reproducibility with comprehensive appendices including full prompts, hyperparameters, and implementation details
Valuable resource contribution with commitment to release datasets for future research
weaknesses: Critical issue: human therapist baseline performs worse than LLMs on most dimensions (2.60 overall quality vs 3.26-4.29, 2.56 toxicity vs 1.36-1.78), suggesting evaluation mismatch or selection bias that undermines benchmark credibility
Limited evaluation scope for main benchmark: only 100 questions across 20 topics (5 per topic) is restrictive for top-tier venue; HealthBench uses tens of thousands of items by comparison
CounselBench-Adv insufficiently validated: only 96 of 3,240 responses (2.96%) manually checked; reliance on GPT-4.1 as labeler for core findings introduces bias given demonstrated LLM judge failures
Medical Advice and Factual Consistency dimensions show notably lower inter-rater reliability (0.72-0.75) compared to other dimensions (0.82-0.83), despite being critical safety metrics

Annotator biases not adequately addressed: experience-dependent differences (empathy scores vary by 0.61 points across experience levels, p=0.02); time-dependent flagging of medical advice suggests potential drift
Limited novelty: multi-dimensional rubric evaluation is established methodology; LLM-as-judge limitations are expected given prior work; identified failure modes are somewhat predictable
Weak actionability for practitioners: paper identifies problems effectively but provides minimal guidance for mitigation, deployment decisions, or practical use of findings

Selection methodology concerns: ranking by upvotes assumes popularity correlates with quality without validation; exclusion of 'sensitive' topics may introduce bias; single data source (CounselChat) limits generalization

Insufficient depth on key findings: superficial treatment of why domain-specific models fail; minimal analysis of why few-shot prompting provides limited improvements (Table 3); limited exploration of implications
Missing important comparisons and baselines: no comparison to automated metrics even as negative controls; limited quantitative comparison to prior medical QA benchmarks
Rubric design not fully justified: no validation that six chosen dimensions correlate with clinical outcomes or therapeutic effectiveness; no ablation studies on dimension selection
Statistical concerns: multiple comparisons without correction (Table 9); restricted analyses reduce power (e.g., 64 QA pairs for experience analysis); effect sizes not reported

strengths: Large-scale expert annotation from 100 verified mental health professionals with 2,000 evaluations and span-level annotations, representing one of the largest expert-annotated datasets for open-ended mental health QA
Clinically grounded evaluation framework with six well-motivated dimensions based on clinical psychology literature and co-designed with psychologists
Rigorous methodology including multiple credential verification methods, three pilot rounds, high inter-rater reliability (K-α ≥ 0.7), and appropriate statistical testing
Important finding demonstrating LLMs systematically overrate peer responses and fail to detect safety concerns (toxicity, factual errors), with minimal variance on safety metrics
Dual-component design providing both breadth (2,000 systematic expert evaluations) and targeted depth (120 adversarial questions) for probing specific failure modes
Comprehensive safety analysis identifying unauthorized medical advice patterns (recommending medications, specific therapy techniques) across models
Strong reproducibility with detailed appendices covering all prompts, hyperparameters, computational resources, and demographic/credential information
Addresses important gap in existing benchmarks by evaluating open-ended mental health QA rather than multiple-choice, reflecting real clinical scenarios
weaknesses: Limited model diversity in main benchmark: only 3 LLMs (GPT-4, LLaMA-3, Gemini) evaluated in COUNSELBENCH-EVAL, limiting generalizability of findings about model rankings and performance patterns
Exclusion of important mental health domains (LGBTQ issues, sexuality, spirituality, religion) due to review concerns reduces benchmark representativeness for clinical deployment
Questionable validity of using forum upvotes as proxy for clinical appropriateness; no validation that upvotes correlate with clinical quality or absence of demographic/style biases
Moderate agreement on adversarial dataset labels (72.9% GPT-4.1 vs. human on 96-response spot check) introduces label noise for 3,240 responses evaluated by GPT-4.1 only
Relatively small question set (100 total across 20 topics) may not capture sufficient variability in mental health issue presentations or topic-specific failure modes
Arbitrary design choices (250-word response limit, top-voted response selection) not validated as representative of clinical practice; may constrain assessment of complex cases
Limited exploration of few-shot prompting findings—failure mode persistence despite examples suggests pretraining issues but mitigation strategies not proposed
Domain-specific model failures (MentalLLaMA, Meditron showing poor performance) discussed only in appendix despite high relevance to model selection recommendations

strengths: Rigorous involvement of 100 credentialed mental health professionals with formal credential verification and comprehensive demographic documentation
Thoughtful two-component benchmark design combining systematic evaluation (EVAL) with targeted adversarial testing (ADV), providing both breadth and depth
Comprehensive expert annotations: 2,000 + 1,080 evaluations with span-level annotations and rich written rationales (median 576.5 words) across 6 clinically-grounded dimensions
Strong inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's α ≥ 0.7) and careful annotation protocol validated through pilot studies
Important practical finding: LLM judges systematically overrate responses and miss safety concerns, particularly toxicity—significant for practitioners
Addresses clear gap in medical QA benchmarking: most existing benchmarks use multiple-choice/factual tasks, not open-ended clinical scenarios
Excellent reproducibility: comprehensive experimental details, hyperparameters, random seeds, prompts, and commitment to release code and data
Real-world grounding using authentic patient questions from CounselChat and verified therapist responses predating widespread LLM use
Clear model-specific failure patterns revealing systematic vulnerabilities (e.g., LLaMA overgeneralizes, Gemini lacks empathy) rather than random errors
Solid statistical analysis with appropriate significance testing, thematic coding of failure modes, and analysis of annotator behavior
weaknesses: Limited scope for foundational benchmark: only 100 base questions across single platform (CounselChat), with excluded sensitive topics (LGBTQ+, intimacy, sexuality, spirituality/religion) representing significant gaps for mental health QA
Single-turn evaluation only; real mental health support often involves multi-turn dialogue for clarification and follow-up, limiting practical applicability
Surprising and underexplored finding: online human therapists score notably lower (2.60 Overall) than LLMs (3.26-4.29), which contradicts expectations and deserves deeper investigation
Limited baseline comparisons: only 3 LLMs in COUNSELBENCH-EVAL; domain-specific models (MentalLLaMA, Meditron) confined to brief pilot (Appendix), with no comparison to non-LLM approaches
Adversarial dataset size and validation: only 120 questions with 2 failure modes per model; limited evidence that adversarial questions consistently elicit targeted failures at elevated rates
Inter-rater reliability for COUNSELBENCH-ADV relegated to appendix; main text should report this critical statistic for the adversarial component
Methodological choices not fully justified: selection of most-upvoted responses as gold standard may favor popularity over clinical quality; binary Medical Advice dimension limits nuanced analysis
LLM-as-judge analysis lacks depth: paper shows LLMs fail but provides limited investigation into causes; few-shot experiments show minimal improvement with insufficient analysis of why
Missing critical analysis: no examination of model performance by patient demographic or question topic; no investigation of whether findings hold across mental health contexts beyond CounselChat
No fairness or bias analysis despite documented annotator demographics; cultural sensitivity and cross-cultural performance not addressed

Key analyses underdeveloped in main text: sentence-level detection results (Table 11) show extremely poor performance with minimal interpretation; surprising findings about human performance lack discussion

strengths: Large-scale expert annotation from 100 licensed mental health professionals with verified credentials, providing 2,000 detailed annotations with median 576.5 words of written rationale per annotator
High inter-rater reliability across most evaluation dimensions (Krippendorff's alpha ≥ 0.7), demonstrating consistent expert judgment
Important and timely focus on open-ended mental health question answering, a realistic and high-stakes application domain under-explored in prior work
Valuable finding demonstrating that LLMs as judges systematically overrate responses and critically fail to detect safety issues like toxicity and unauthorized medical advice
Empirically-grounded adversarial dataset derived from observed failures in COUNSELBENCH-EVAL rather than predefined literature-driven failure modes
Comprehensive reproducibility documentation including detailed prompts, hyperparameters, annotation protocols, and commitment to publicly release benchmark resources
Diverse annotator expertise spanning 32 credential types and 43 specialized counseling areas
Rich annotation data including span-level labels and detailed written rationales enabling nuanced analysis of response quality
weaknesses: Limited novelty in evaluation framework; the six dimensions are straightforward and similar multi-dimensional rubrics already exist in MultiMedQA and HealthBench, with the primary contribution being application to a new domain rather than methodological innovation
Significant dataset limitations: single source (CounselChat), only 100 questions, all responses artificially capped at 250 words, pre-2022 data does not reflect recent LLM capability advances
Framework explicitly designed for single-turn interactions only, severely restricting applicability to real clinical dialogue where multi-turn context is essential

Weak adversarial benchmark component: only 120 questions total with LLM judges achieving F1 scores ≤ 0.50 for failure-mode detection; few-shot experiments show minimal improvements without explanation
No external validation that the six evaluation dimensions actually correlate with clinical outcomes, patient wellbeing, or real-world therapeutic effectiveness
Moderate inter-rater reliability on safety-critical dimensions (K-α = 0.72-0.75 for Toxicity and Factual Consistency), raising concerns about measurement reliability for high-stakes applications
Primarily descriptive work identifying LLM problems without proposing solutions, improvements, or actionable guidance for practitioners and researchers
Questionable methodological choices: using CounselChat upvotes as proxy for clinical quality, limited model diversity (3 LLMs in EVAL), and weak human baseline from public forum responses
Qualitative failure analysis relies on GPT-4.1 to categorize human rationales, introducing automation bias and potentially missing clinical nuances
No analysis of which failure modes correlate with clinical harm or patient outcomes; all dimensions treated as equally important
Limited generalizability: unclear if findings transfer to other medical domains, multi-turn settings, or diverse demographic groups
No direct comparison with or evaluation on existing mental health QA benchmarks (MHQA, PsyQA), making incremental value difficult to assess
Single disclaimer stating 'not for clinical use' may be insufficient for a safety-critical application involving vulnerable populations

strengths: Addresses important gap: First large-scale expert-annotated benchmark for open-ended mental health QA (vs. multiple-choice proxies)

Exceptional quality expert participation: 100 licensed professionals with verified credentials, diverse specializations (77 depression/anxiety, 62 trauma), rigorous verification methods, high engagement (576.5 median words in rationales)

Clinically grounded evaluation: Six evidence-based dimensions (empathy, specificity, medical advice, factual consistency, toxicity) with high inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff α≥0.7), span-level annotations enable nuanced analysis

Critical safety findings: Identifies LLM limitations in mental health (unconstructive feedback, overgeneralization, unauthorized medical advice), shows LLMs systematically overrate responses and miss safety concerns when used as judges
Comprehensive dataset design: 2,000 annotations (100 questions × 4 answers × 5 raters), randomized response ordering, blind annotation, fair comparison across models
Novel adversarial component: 120 expert-authored questions derived from empirical failures in EVAL, reveals model-specific patterns (e.g., therapy suggestions: GPT-5 0.85 vs Llama 0.55-0.65)
Methodological rigor: Pilot studies, Wilcoxon tests, comprehensive implementation details, commitment to data/code release, IRB approval with proper ethics
Balanced qualitative-quantitative analysis: Thematic coding of rationales yields seven failure categories with frequency distribution, well-integrated into findings
Broader applicability: Framework and clinically grounded rubric generalizable to other therapeutic domains and medical QA tasks
weaknesses: Limited dataset scope: Only 100 questions from single source (CounselChat pre-2022), homogeneous annotators (84% female, 75% white, all US-based), excluded sensitive topics (LGBTQ, intimacy), raises generalization concerns to other platforms/cultures/languages
Single-turn limitation: Framework restricted to single-turn Q&A by design, but real therapy is multi-turn; acknowledged but limits applicability to conversational systems

Evaluation dimension design: Medical Advice binary (doesn't capture severity), inconsistent scales (binary vs. 4-point vs. 5-point), Factual Consistency has lowest agreement (α=0.75), 'I'm not sure' responses excluded underrepresent uncertainty
Limited model coverage: EVAL covers only 3 models (GPT-4, LLaMA, Gemini), domain-specific models poorly evaluated due to task misalignment, no medical-specialized foundation models
Statistical rigor gaps: Multiple comparisons without explicit correction, no effect sizes reported, no power analysis, Table 9 shows experience affects ratings but causality unclear

Adversarial design concerns: Only 120 adversarial questions (comparable to EVAL component), two failure modes per model seems arbitrary, limited validation that targeted modes represent broad failure space
Limited novelty on LLM-as-judge: Findings (overrating, missing toxicity) align with prior work; confirmation valuable but not deeply exploring mechanisms or solutions

Problem identification without solutions: Identifies issues well but provides limited guidance for fixing them; few-shot experiments show minimal improvements with no alternative interventions explored (RLHF, fine-tuning)

Medical advice validation: No domain expert validation of flagged advice authenticity; risk of false positives for appropriate clinical guidance; span extraction reliant on copy-paste (Table 12 shows unmatched fragments)

Missing depth on practical implications: Limited discussion of clinical outcome relevance, patient safety in practice, or actionable guidance for LLM developers; primarily descriptive/benchmarking work
